name: Purpose
tagline: A mental wellness app built around guided reflection, mood check-ins, and habit nudges meant to help you figure out what you actually care about.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Strip away the branding and this category is a journal with a mood field, a prompt library, and a streak counter, which an agent will produce before your coffee gets cold. The part that does not come free is the content: the sequencing of exercises, the writing quality of the prompts, and whatever clinical review sits behind them. Also worth saying plainly: the paid app is not therapy either, so "needs human oversight" is an argument for talking to a person, not an argument for the subscription. Where the DIY build genuinely falls short is the phone: real push reminders, offline sync, and a widget are the difference between a habit and an abandoned tab. Build it if you want private data and your own prompts, pay if the structured program is the thing doing the work.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you log a daily mood plus a written reflection against a rotating prompt, tag entries by value or goal, and see streaks and mood trends over time.
requirements: A machine to run it on, phone access via local network or a private deploy
Optional LLM API key if you want generated reflection prompts instead of a fixed pack
whatYouLose: Real mobile push notifications, widgets, and offline sync, which is most of what makes a wellness habit stick
A professionally written and sequenced exercise library instead of prompts you or a model made up
Any clinical framing or safety escalation, a homemade journal has no crisis handling at all
Cross-device sync and encrypted backup unless you build and maintain it
The mild accountability of having paid for something
moatNotes: The defensible asset in this category is the written program and whoever signed off on it, not the mood chart.
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay because the structure is the product. A blank journal with a text box is free and has always been free, and most people still do not use it. What a subscription buys is a sequence someone else decided on, a reminder that arrives on your lock screen, and the feeling that a considered method is behind the questions you are being asked. A self-built version gives you total privacy and prompts you control, which matters to some people quite a lot, but it also gives you a project to maintain at exactly the moments you are least inclined to maintain anything.
notes: The journal is trivial; the curriculum and the 8am reminder are the actual product.
prompt:
Build a private, local-first mental wellness journal called "Compass". Single user, no accounts, no telemetry, no cloud.

Stack, non negotiable: Next.js 15 with the App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind, SQLite through better-sqlite3 with a file at ./data/compass.db. Server actions for writes. No ORM, write the SQL.

Data model:
- entries: id, created_at, mood_score 1 to 5, energy_score 1 to 5, prompt_id, body text, tags (comma separated)
- prompts: id, text, theme, active
- values: id, label, note (the small set of things the user says they care about)
- habits: id, label, active; habit_logs: id, habit_id, date, done

Seed prompts.json with 60 reflection prompts spread across themes: values, gratitude, friction, work, relationships, body, meaning. Write them yourself, plain and specific, no horoscope language. Seed on first run only.

Screens:
1. Today: the day's prompt (deterministic from the date so it does not reshuffle on refresh), mood and energy sliders, a textarea, value tags as toggle chips, habit checkboxes. One save button. Saving twice on the same day edits the existing entry.
2. History: reverse chronological list, full text search over body, filter by tag and by mood range.
3. Trends: 30 and 90 day mood and energy line charts, habit completion grid, most used tags. Use a tiny inline SVG chart component, do not add a charting library.
4. Settings: edit values, edit habits, add or disable prompts, export everything to JSON, import it back.

Rules:
- Everything works offline against localhost. No external network calls in the default build.
- If OPENAI_API_KEY exists in .env.local, add one optional button on Today: "generate a prompt from my recent entries". Absent key means the button is not rendered. Nothing else touches the network.
- Add a PWA manifest and a service worker that caches the shell so it installs on a phone over LAN.
- Do not fake push notifications. Put one line in the README telling the user to set a recurring alarm on their phone, because browser reminders on iOS will not fire reliably.
- Include a static footer line: this is a journal, not treatment, and list no crisis numbers you cannot verify.

Deliver: working app, seeded db on first run, README with setup, and a .env.example with the optional key commented out.
